confidence-interval-calculator.assumptionNote: Uses the normal (z) approximation: fine for large samples. For small samples (n under 30) a t-distribution interval is more accurate - treat these results as approximate.
benefits: Turns a sample mean into an honest range instead of a false single number.
Both modes covered: means (test scores, weights) and proportions (polls, conversion rates).
Shows the margin of error and standard error, not just the interval.
90%, 95%, and 99% levels with one tap - no z-table lookup needed.

faqs.a: It means: if you repeated the sampling the same way many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value. It does NOT mean there is a 95% chance the true value is inside this particular interval.
Yes. The margin of error shrinks with the square root of n, so quadrupling the sample halves the margin. That is why polls of 1,000 people quote about ±3 points.
faqs.q: Does a bigger sample give a narrower interval?

faqs.a: A smaller margin (tighter interval). 90% uses z = 1.645 instead of 1.96, so the interval narrows - but you accept a 1-in-10 chance of missing the true value instead of 1-in-20.
Standard error = standard deviation / sqrt(n). It measures how much sample means wobble around the true mean. The margin of error is just z times the standard error.
For a proportion of 0.6 with n = 400 at 95%: SE = sqrt(0.6 x 0.4 / 400) = 0.0245, margin = 1.96 x 0.0245 = 0.048, so the interval is 0.552 to 0.648 (55.2% to 64.8%).
faqs.q: How is the proportion example computed?

faqs.a: The Wald interval collapses to zero width there, which is misleading. Exact methods (Clopper-Pearson) handle the edges properly - this tool warns you instead of pretending.

confidence-interval-calculator.formula:
Mean: CI = x-bar ± z x (s / sqrt(n))
Proportion: CI = p-hat ± z x sqrt(p-hat x (1 - p-hat) / n)
z-values: 90% -> 1.645, 95% -> 1.96, 99% -> 2.576
Example: 50 ± 1.96 x (10 / 10) = 50 ± 1.96 = (48.04, 51.96)
howTo: Choose the mode: Mean (averages) or Proportion (percentages).
For a mean: enter the sample mean, standard deviation, and sample size.
For a proportion: enter it as a decimal (0.6 for 60%) plus the sample size.
Pick 90%, 95%, or 99% confidence and read the interval, margin, and standard error.
keyFacts: The interval = estimate ± z x standard error.
Quadrupling the sample size halves the margin of error.
A 95% CI does not mean a 95% chance the truth is inside this interval.
For a proportion, enter it as a decimal: 0.6 means 60%.

limitations: Uses the normal (z) approximation - small samples really need the t-distribution.
Assumes a roughly normal sampling distribution and independent observations.
The proportion mode uses the Wald interval, which misbehaves near 0 and 1.
Garbage in, garbage out: a biased sample gives a precisely wrong interval.
